title: Arachnids of medical importance: the village tick, the scabies mite, the dog and taiga ticks. Insects of medical importance: lice, fleas, mosquitoes, flies, sandflies. Venomous animals

goals.text: To teach the student the general features and classification of the phylum Arthropoda, the medically important members of the classes Arachnida and Insecta — their structure, development, the diseases they spread and the measures used to control them — and the venomous animals found in Uzbekistan and first aid for their bites and stings.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general features and classification of arthropods;
the structure and medical importance of argasid and ixodid ticks and the scabies mite;
the medical importance of lice, fleas, bedbugs, cockroaches, mosquitoes, sandflies, flies and horseflies;
the concepts of specific and mechanical vectors, transovarial transmission and natural focality;
the classification of venomous animals and first aid for their bites and stings.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish argasid and ixodid ticks, lice and fleas in preparations;
tell the malaria mosquito from the common mosquito at every stage of development;
explain the procedure for first aid after a bite or sting by a venomous animal.

blocks.text: **Arthropods (Arthropoda)** are the largest phylum of the animal kingdom. General features: the body and legs are **jointed**, the external skeleton is a **chitinous** cuticle, growth takes place by **moulting**, the body cavity is mixed (**mixocoel**), and the circulatory system is open. Three subphyla matter for medicine: the **gill-breathers** (crustaceans — Cyclops and crabs are intermediate hosts of helminths), the **chelicerates** (arachnids) and the **tracheates** (insects).

**Arachnids (Arachnida)** have a body divided into a **cephalothorax** and an **abdomen**, 4 pairs of walking legs, chelicerae and pedipalps around the mouth, and no antennae. Of medical importance are scorpions, spiders and especially the order of **ticks and mites (Acari)**. Ticks and mites are divided into the **acariform** group (the scabies mite and the follicle mite — *Demodex*) and the **parasitiform** group (argasid and ixodid ticks). Tick development: egg → **larva** (3 pairs of legs) → **nymph** → **imago** (4 pairs of legs).

blocks.text: **Transovarial and transstadial transmission in ticks:** the pathogen multiplies in the tick and passes through the egg to the next generation (**transovarial**) and from larva to nymph and from nymph to imago (**transstadial**). Ticks are therefore not only vectors but also **natural reservoirs** of the pathogen. Academician **Ye.N. Pavlovsky** developed the doctrine of the **natural focality** of vector-borne diseases: the pathogen circulates among wild animals and vectors independently of humans.

**The scabies mite** (*Sarcoptes scabiei*) is the agent of **scabies**; it measures 0.3–0.4 mm. The female burrows tunnels in the stratum corneum of the skin and lays her eggs there. Favourite sites are the spaces between the fingers, the wrists, abdomen and inner thighs. The main sign is **itching that worsens at night**. Transmission — direct skin contact, shared bedding and clothing. Diagnosis — finding the mite in a scraping taken from a burrow.

sections.title: 2. Class Insecta. Lice, fleas, bedbugs, cockroaches

blocks.text: **Insects (Insecta)** have a body consisting of a **head**, **thorax** and **abdomen**; the thorax bears 3 pairs of legs and usually 2 pairs of wings, and the head 1 pair of antennae; they breathe through tracheae. Development is of two kinds: with **incomplete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → imago: lice, bedbugs, cockroaches) and with **complete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → **pupa** → imago: fleas, Diptera).

**Lice (Anoplura)** are wingless permanent ectoparasites that feed only on human blood throughout their life (Figure 14.2). Three species parasitize humans: the **head louse** (*Pediculus humanus capitis*), the **body louse** (*P. h. corporis*) and the **pubic louse** (*Phthirus pubis*). A louse feeds 2–3 times a day for 3–10 minutes each time; the female lays 6–14 eggs (nits) a day, gluing them to hair or clothing fibres; development from egg to imago takes 16–20 days. Louse infestation is called **pediculosis**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Lice: a — male head louse; b — female head louse; c — pubic louse clinging to a hair; d — louse engorged with blood (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **The body louse** is the vector of epidemic **typhus** (*Rickettsia prowazekii*) and epidemic **relapsing fever** (*Borrelia recurrentis*). The pathogens are not transmitted with saliva when the louse bites: in typhus the rickettsiae are passed in the louse's **faeces** and rubbed into scratched skin; in relapsing fever the borreliae are in the louse's haemolymph and enter skin wounds **when the louse is crushed**. In wars, famine and breakdowns of hygiene these diseases become epidemic.

blocks.text: **Fleas (Siphonaptera)** are wingless insects, flattened from side to side, with jumping legs; they develop with complete metamorphosis, and their larvae live in floor cracks and rubbish. **The rat flea** (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) is the vector of **plague** (*Yersinia pestis*): the bacteria form a “block” in the flea's proventriculus and are regurgitated into the wound when it feeds. **The human flea** (*Pulex irritans*) can also carry plague.

**The bedbug** (*Cimex lectularius*) feeds at night, and its bites cause itching and allergy. **Cockroaches** (*Blattella germanica, Periplaneta americana*) are **mechanical carriers** of intestinal infections, helminth eggs and protozoan cysts; their chitin remains and secretions are strong **allergens** that cause bronchial asthma and allergic reactions in children.

**Diptera** are insects with one pair of membranous wings, the second pair having become vibrating halteres; they develop with complete metamorphosis. They are divided into two suborders: the **long-horned** (mosquitoes, sandflies, black flies — *Simulium*) and the **short-horned** (flies, horseflies).

blocks.text: ***Aedes*** mosquitoes carry the dengue, yellow fever and Zika viruses. **Sandflies** (*Phlebotomus*) are small and hairy and breed in rodent burrows in hot regions; they are the vectors of the **leishmaniases** (cutaneous and visceral) and of sandfly (pappataci) fever. **Black flies** (*Simulium*) carry onchocerciasis.

**The housefly** (*Musca domestica*) is a **mechanical carrier** of intestinal infections (dysentery, typhoid fever, cholera), helminth eggs and protozoan cysts: microbes are carried on the sticky hairs of its feet, on its proboscis and in its gut, and reach food in vomit and faeces. **Wohlfahrt's fly** (*Wohlfahrtia magnifica*) deposits live larvae in wounds, ears, nose and eyes — causing **obligate myiasis**. **The stable fly** (*Stomoxys calcitrans*) and **horseflies** (*Tabanidae*) suck blood but are only **mechanical** carriers of anthrax and tularaemia. **The tsetse fly** (*Glossina*) carries sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) in Africa.

items: **Specific (biological) vector** — the pathogen multiplies in it or completes part of its life cycle there (Anopheles — malaria, sandfly — Leishmania, louse — rickettsia, tick — encephalitis virus).
**Mechanical carrier** — the pathogen stays unchanged in the carrier and is merely transferred on its body surface or proboscis (housefly, cockroach, horsefly, stable fly).

blocks.text: **Venomous animals** produce or accumulate substances that are toxic to humans and animals. **Primarily venomous** animals produce venom in special glands themselves; they are either **actively armed** (with a venom gland and a stinging or biting apparatus: snakes, scorpions, spiders, wasps) or **passive** (with venom glands but no delivery apparatus: frogs, some fish). **Secondarily venomous** animals accumulate toxins from their food (some fish and molluscs). By their action, venoms are **neurotoxic** (acting on the nervous system) or **haemotoxic** (acting on the blood and vessels).

parts.text: **First aid for snakebite:** calm the patient and lay them down; immobilize the bitten limb with a splint; remove rings and bracelets; give plenty of fluids; take the patient to hospital urgently — there **snake antivenom** is given. **Do not:** apply a tourniquet, cut or cauterize the wound, or give alcohol. For a karakurt bite, **anti-karakurt serum** is used.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing argasid and ixodid ticks in a preparation

items: Examine the tick from the dorsal side with a magnifier or the low-power objective of a microscope.
Determine whether there is a chitinous scutum on the back.
Check whether the mouthparts (capitulum) are visible from above or hidden under the body.
No scutum and mouthparts not visible from above — conclude an argasid tick; scutum present and mouthparts visible at the front end — an ixodid tick.
Count the legs to identify the stage: 3 pairs — larva, 4 pairs — nymph or imago (the nymph has no genital opening).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Scabies was found in most of the students sent to pick cotton.
cases.ask: Explain the reasons. What measures can eliminate the disease?
cases.answer: The scabies mite, *Sarcoptes scabiei*, is transmitted by direct skin contact, shared beds, bedding and clothing. Crowded living in dormitories, sleeping on shared bedding and limited opportunities to wash and change clothes caused the disease to spread quickly. Measures: treating all patients and their contacts at the same time (permethrin, benzyl benzoate), boiling or hot-ironing underwear and bedding, isolating patients, examining contacts and improving sanitary and hygienic conditions.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A tick taken from an animal was examined under the microscope: no chitinous scutum was found on its back, and its mouthparts are not visible from above. Among other ticks, there are also specimens in which the pathogen was found even though they had not fed on blood.
cases.ask: Which family does this tick belong to? How can the presence of the pathogen in ticks that have not fed be explained?
cases.answer: The absence of a scutum and the position of the mouthparts on the underside of the body are typical of argasid ticks (*Argasidae*), for example the village tick — the vector of tick-borne relapsing fever. The pathogen in unfed ticks is explained by transovarial transmission: the pathogen multiplies in the mother tick and passes through the egg to the next generation, and it is also retained from larva to nymph and imago by the transstadial route. Ticks are therefore natural reservoirs of the pathogen.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A person bitten by a snake has bleeding from the bite site, severe pain, rapidly spreading swelling and a sharp fall in blood pressure. Another patient, after a snakebite, developed difficulty breathing and swallowing, numbness of the body and difficulty moving.
cases.ask: In each case, what kind of snake might be suspected?
cases.answer: The first case shows the effect of a haemotoxic venom — impaired blood clotting, damage to the vessel walls and local tissue necrosis; this is seen after bites by vipers such as the Levant viper (gyurza), the saw-scaled viper or the Halys pit viper. The second case shows the effect of a neurotoxic venom — blockade of neuromuscular transmission, paralysis and respiratory failure; this is seen after a bite by the Central Asian cobra. In both cases the limb is immobilized, no tourniquet is applied, and the patient is taken urgently to hospital and given snake antivenom; in neurotoxic poisoning one must be ready for artificial ventilation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In a **specific vector** the pathogen multiplies or develops; a **mechanical carrier** only transfers it — even if it sucks blood (horsefly, stable fly).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Argasid — armourless, Ixodid — shielded”**; **“Anopheles — Angled at rest, Culex — Calmly parallel”**.

summary.label: Clinical relevance
summary.text: After a snakebite **no tourniquet and no cutting**: immobilization and urgent antivenom are the main life-saving measures.
